claim: POm provides axonal projections to the dorsal striatum.
source: POm provides axonal projections to the dorsal striatum, a hotspot of sensorimotor processing, yet the role of POm-striatal projections has remained undetermined.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a known anatomical fact.

claim: POm provides robust synaptic input to direct pathway striatal spiny projection neurons (D1-SPNs).
source: Using optogenetics with mouse brain slice electrophysiology, we found that POm provides robust synaptic input to direct and indirect pathway striatal spiny projection neurons (D1- and D2-SPNs, respectively) and parvalbumin-expressing fast spiking interneurons (PVs).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from optogenetic stimulation and electrophysiological recordings presented in the manuscript.

claim: POm provides robust synaptic input to indirect pathway striatal spiny projection neurons (D2-SPNs).
source: Using optogenetics with mouse brain slice electrophysiology, we found that POm provides robust synaptic input to direct and indirect pathway striatal spiny projection neurons (D1- and D2-SPNs, respectively) and parvalbumin-expressing fast spiking interneurons (PVs).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from optogenetic stimulation and electrophysiological recordings presented in the manuscript.

claim: POm provides robust synaptic input to parvalbumin-expressing fast spiking interneurons (PVs).
source: Using optogenetics with mouse brain slice electrophysiology, we found that POm provides robust synaptic input to direct and indirect pathway striatal spiny projection neurons (D1- and D2-SPNs, respectively) and parvalbumin-expressing fast spiking interneurons (PVs).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from optogenetic stimulation and electrophysiological recordings presented in the manuscript.

claim: POm-striatal projections displayed learning-related activation during the performance of a whisker-based tactile discrimination task.
source: During the performance of a whisker-based tactile discrimination task in head-restrained mice, POm-striatal projections displayed learning-related activation correlating with anticipatory, but not reward-related, pupil dilation.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo fiber photometry data collected during behavioral task performance.

claim: POm-striatal activation correlates with anticipatory pupil dilation.
source: During the performance of a whisker-based tactile discrimination task in head-restrained mice, POm-striatal projections displayed learning-related activation correlating with anticipatory, but not reward-related, pupil dilation.
evidence: This claim is supported by simultaneous recording of POm-striatal calcium signals and pupil dynamics during behavior.

claim: POm-striatal activation does not correlate with reward-related pupil dilation.
source: During the performance of a whisker-based tactile discrimination task in head-restrained mice, POm-striatal projections displayed learning-related activation correlating with anticipatory, but not reward-related, pupil dilation.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of POm-striatal calcium signals during reward delivery phases of the behavioral task.

claim: Inhibition of POm-striatal axons across learning caused slower reaction times.
source: Inhibition of POm-striatal axons across learning caused slower reaction times and an increase in the number of training sessions for expert performance.
evidence: This claim is supported by optogenetic inhibition experiments during behavioral task performance.

claim: Inhibition of POm-striatal axons across learning caused an increase in the number of training sessions for expert performance.
source: Inhibition of POm-striatal axons across learning caused slower reaction times and an increase in the number of training sessions for expert performance.
evidence: This claim is supported by optogenetic inhibition experiments during behavioral task performance.

claim: POm-striatal inputs provide a behaviorally relevant arousal-related signal.
source: Our data indicate that POm-striatal inputs provide a behaviorally relevant arousal-related signal, which may prime striatal circuitry for efficient integration of subsequent choice-related inputs.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the experimental data presented in the manuscript, including photometry and optogenetic manipulation results.

claim: POm-striatal inputs may prime striatal circuitry for efficient integration of subsequent choice-related inputs.
source: Our data indicate that POm-striatal inputs provide a behaviorally relevant arousal-related signal, which may prime striatal circuitry for efficient integration of subsequent choice-related inputs.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the experimental findings.

claim: Tactile sensations in the mouse whisker system are acquired via active sensor movement.
source: In the mouse whisker system, tactile sensations are acquired via active sensor (e.g. whisker) movement to obtain relevant environmental information and subsequent processing by the well-characterized primary somatosensory barrel cortex (S1) circuitry (Petersen, 2019; El-Boustani et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Whisker-related information is transmitted from the periphery to S1 via VPM and POm thalamic nuclei.
source: This whisker-related information is transmitted from the periphery to S1 via two thalamic nuclei, ventral posterior medial (VPM) and posterior medial (POm), constituting the lemniscal and paralemniscal pathways, respectively (Deschênes et al., 2003; Bureau et al., 2006; Petersen, 2007; Diamond et al., 2008; Moore et al., 2015; Deschenes and Urbain, 2016; Yu et al., 2006; Mo et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: VPM and POm constitute the lemniscal and paralemniscal pathways, respectively.
source: This whisker-related information is transmitted from the periphery to S1 via two thalamic nuclei, ventral posterior medial (VPM) and posterior medial (POm), constituting the lemniscal and paralemniscal pathways, respectively (Deschênes et al., 2003; Bureau et al., 2006; Petersen, 2007; Diamond et al., 2008; Moore et al., 2015; Deschenes and Urbain, 2016; Yu et al., 2006; Mo et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: VPM reliably encodes fast-whisking components including self-motion and tactile information.
source: VPM reliably encodes fast-whisking components including self-motion and tactile information (Moore et al., 2015; Chiaia et al., 1991b; Diamond et al., 1992; Sosnik et al., 2001; Urbain et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: POm encodes phase-related whisking activity with relatively lower magnitude responses and higher response failure rates.
source: Conversely, POm encodes phase-related whisking activity with relatively lower magnitude responses and higher response failure rates (Moore et al., 2015; Diamond et al., 1992; Sosnik et al., 2001; Urbain et al., 2015; Chiaia et al., 1991a; Lavallée et al., 2005; Masri et al., 2008; Petty et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: POm is activated during changes in behavioral state, especially related to sensory and nociceptive processing.
source: Recent work has highlighted two behavior-related aspects of POm function: (1) activation during changes in behavioral state, especially related to sensory and nociceptive processing (Moore et al., 2015; Chiaia et al., 1991b; Diamond et al., 1992; Sosnik et al., 2001; Masri et al., 2008; Petty et al., 2021; Noseda et al., 2010; Frangeul et al., 2014; Osaki et al., 2022)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: POm drives learning-related plasticity at its cortical synapses.
source: (2) driving learning-related plasticity at its cortical synapses (Gambino et al., 2014; Audette et al., 2019; Williams and Holtmaat, 2019; Zhang and Bruno, 2019; La Terra et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: POm receives glutamatergic inputs from S1, M1, secondary somatosensory cortex, superior colliculus, and spinal trigeminal interpolaris.
source: POm receives a plethora of inputs including glutamatergic (S1, primary motor cortex (M1), secondary somatosensory cortex, superior colliculus, and spinal trigeminal interpolaris; Chiaia et al., 1991a; Roger and Cadusseau, 1984; Pierret et al., 2000; Alloway et al., 2003; Alloway et al., 2008; Groh et al., 2014; Yamawaki and Shepherd, 2015; Sumser et al., 2017; Gharaei et al., 2020)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: POm receives GABAergic inputs from ventral zona incerta, anterior pretectal nucleus, and thalamic reticular nucleus.
source: GABAergic (ventral zona incerta, anterior pretectal nucleus, and thalamic reticular nucleus; Lavallée et al., 2005; Roger and Cadusseau, 1985; Power et al., 1999; Barthó et al., 2002; Power and Mitrofanis, 2002; Trageser and Keller, 2004; Barthó et al., 2007; Giber et al., 2008; Watson et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: POm receives cholinergic inputs from pedunculopontine and laterodorsal tegmental nuclei.
source: and cholinergic (pedunculopontine and laterodorsal tegmental nuclei; Masri et al., 2006; Trageser et al., 2006; Park et al., 2017; Huerta-Ocampo et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: The stereotypical POm-cortical projection terminates in S1 layers 1 and L5A.
source: Further, the stereotypical POm-cortical projection terminates in S1, specifically layers (L)1 and L5A (Bureau et al., 2006; Meyer et al., 2010; Wimmer et al., 2010; Ohno et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: POm-cortical projections have been studied in the context of driving cortical plasticity/perceptual learning.
source: and has been studied in the context of driving cortical plasticity/perceptual learning (Gambino et al., 2014; Audette et al., 2019; Williams and Holtmaat, 2019; Zhang and Bruno, 2019; La Terra et al., 2022; Audette et al., 2018; Qi et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: POm axons pass through and collateralize with terminal synaptic boutons in thalamic reticular nucleus and posterior dorsolateral striatum.
source: In addition to its cortical projection, POm axons pass through and collateralize with terminal synaptic boutons in both thalamic reticular nucleus and posterior dorsolateral striatum (pDLS) as they ascend toward cortex (Ohno et al., 2012; Spreafico et al., 1987; Descheˆnes et al., 1995; Viaene et al., 2011; Smith et al., 2012; Alloway et al., 2017; Li et al., 2020; O'Reilly et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: The striatum is the predominant input nucleus of the basal ganglia.
source: The striatum is the predominant input nucleus of the basal ganglia and is predominantly composed of GABAergic spiny projection neurons (SPNs) expressing either D1 or D2 dopamine receptors (Gerfen et al., 1996; Gerfen and Surmeier, 2011; Tritsch and Sabatini, 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The striatum is predominantly composed of GABAergic spiny projection neurons expressing either D1 or D2 dopamine receptors.
source: The striatum is the predominant input nucleus of the basal ganglia and is predominantly composed of GABAergic spiny projection neurons (SPNs) expressing either D1 or D2 dopamine receptors (Gerfen et al., 1996; Gerfen and Surmeier, 2011; Tritsch and Sabatini, 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Parvalbumin-expressing fast-spiking interneurons exert robust modulatory control over SPN output.
source: but it also contains a rich diversity of interneurons, such as parvalbumin-expressing (PV) fast-spiking interneurons that exert robust modulatory control over SPN output (Gittis et al., 2010; Tepper et al., 2010; Lee et al., 2017; Owen et al., 2018; Tepper et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: The dorsal striatum integrates widespread convergent cortical and thalamic inputs.
source: Within this microcircuitry, the dorsal striatum integrates widespread convergent cortical and thalamic inputs that constitute part of the force driving normal striatal functioning (Pan et al., 2010; Wall et al., 2013; Huerta-Ocampo et al., 2014; Oh et al., 2014; Guo et al., 2015; Hunnicutt et al., 2016; Hintiryan et al., 2016; Smith et al., 2016; Hooks et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Functionally related cortical (S1 and M1) and thalamic (POm) inputs converge within shared striatal subregions.
source: Notably, functionally related cortical (S1 and M1) and thalamic (POm) inputs converge within shared striatal subregions (Hunnicutt et al., 2016; Hintiryan et al., 2016; Alexander et al., 1986).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: M1 and S1 are heavily interconnected via reciprocal L2/3 and L5 connections.
source: For example, M1 and S1 are heavily interconnected via reciprocal L2/3 and L5 connections, (Mao et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2013a; Kwon et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: M1 and S1 projections overlap within dorsal striatum and even onto the same neuron.
source: and their projections overlap within dorsal striatum and even onto the same neuron (Hunnicutt et al., 2016; Alloway et al., 2000; Hoffer and Alloway, 2001; Ramanathan et al., 2002; Charpier et al., 2020; Smith et al., 2022; Sanabria et al., 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Striatal inputs have been shown to differ anatomically.
source: While some studies treat striatal inputs as a uniform entity (Ding et al., 2008; Doig et al., 2014), they have been shown to differ anatomically (Hunnicutt et al., 2016; Hintiryan et al., 2016; Hooks et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Striatal inputs have been shown to differ functionally.
source: functionally (Lee et al., 2019; Johansson and Silberberg, 2020)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Striatal inputs have been shown to differ behaviorally.
source: and behaviorally (Lee et al., 2019; Sun et al., 2021; Zareian et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: The most prominent thalamostriatal modulation occurs via parafascicular (Pf) thalamus.
source: The most prominent thalamostriatal modulation occurs via parafascicular (Pf) thalamus (Johansson and Silberberg, 2020; Smith and Parent, 1986; Berendse and Groenewegen, 1990; Lapper and Bolam, 1992; Matsumoto et al., 2001; Ellender et al., 2013; Parker et al., 2016; Mandelbaum et al., 2019; Tanimura et al., 2019; Fallon et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Pf is implicated in regulating action flexibility.
source: Pf is implicated in regulating action flexibility (Brown et al., 2010; Bradfield et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Pf contributes to the initiation and execution of learned sequences of movements.
source: and contributing to the initiation and execution of learned sequences of movements (Fallon et al., 2023; Díaz-Hernández et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Pf robustly innervates striatal cholinergic interneurons.
source: through its robust innervation of striatal cholinergic interneurons (Lapper and Bolam, 1992; Ding et al., 2008; Doig et al., 2014; Johansson and Silberberg, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Optogenetic activation of POm terminals readily elicited depolarizing postsynaptic potentials in all targeted cell types.
source: Optogenetic activation of POm terminals readily elicited depolarizing postsynaptic potentials (PSP) in all targeted cell types (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Responses to single pulse stimulation resulted in relatively equal PSP amplitudes for D1-SPNs (7.05±0.75 mV), D2-SPNs (8.79±1.67 mV), PVs (10.83±1.91 mV), and putative SPNs (5.54±1.04 mV).
source: Responses to SP stimulation resulted in relatively equal PSP amplitudes for D1-SPNs (7.05±0.75 mV), D2-SPNs (8.79±1.67 mV), PVs (10.83±1.91 mV), and neighboring unlabeled cells that we termed putative SPNs, based on their intrinsic firing properties (5.54±1.04 mV) (F(4,51) = 2.455, p=0.4835; Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The latency to maximum PSP amplitude was significantly shorter in PVs (7.29±0.32ms) than D1-SPNs (11.05±0.45ms), D2-SPNs (10.68±0.56ms), and putative SPNs (10.81±0.92ms).
source: The latency to maximum PSP amplitude was significantly shorter in PVs (7.29±0.32ms, n=17 cells from 7 mice) than D1-SPNs (11.05±0.45ms, n=20 cells from 6 mice), D2-SPNs (10.68±0.56ms, n=11 cells from 5 mice), and putative SPNs (10.81±0.92ms, n=7 cells from 4 mice; F(4,51) = 29.78, p<0.0001, PV vs. D1 p<0.0001, PV vs. D2 p=0.0003, PV vs. SPN, p=0.0056; Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: All cell types exhibited robust synaptic depression overall in response to paired-pulse ratio stimulation.
source: While all cell types exhibited robust synaptic depression overall, no PPR differences were observed (D1-SPNs: 0.73±0.03, n=20, D2-SPNs: 0.72±0.05, n=11, PVs: 0.86±0.05, n=17, SPNs: 0.71±0.08, n=7; F(4,51) = 7.101, p=0.0688; Figure 1I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: PV interneurons exhibited a milder synaptic depression relative to both SPN types during train stimulation.
source: Similar to PPR stimulation, train stimulation elicited overall synaptic depression in all cell types, but PV interneurons exhibited a milder synaptic depression relative to both SPN types that occurred predominantly between pulses 5–15 (Figure 1L, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1L and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: PV interneurons (0.49±0.05) showed significant differences in train stimulation response compared to D1-SPNs (0.30±0.03) and D2-SPNs (0.28±0.03), but not with SPNs (0.31±0.06).
source: PV interneurons (0.49±0.05, n=17) showed significant differences compared to D1-SPNs (0.30±0.03, n=20) and D2-SPNs (0.28±0.03, n=11), but not with SPNs (0.31±0.06; F(4,51) = 10.99, p=0.0118, D1-SPN vs. PV p=0.0184, D2-SPN vs. PV p=0.0481, PV vs. SPN p=0.4940; Figure 1L).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1L.

claim: Mice in the fiber photometry cohort rapidly learned to discriminate between the two textures.
source: Thus, the FP cohort rapidly learned to discriminate between the two textures as validated by behavioral responding parameters.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data showing increased Hit rate and decreased FA rate across training sessions.

claim: It took the fiber photometry cohort 7.6±0.51 sessions on average to become Experts.
source: On average, it took this cohort 7.6±0.51 sessions to become Experts (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The average maximum calcium amplitude significantly increased across learning.
source: First, the average maximum calcium amplitude significantly increased across learning (F(1.818,7.271)=39.24, p=0.0001, n=5; Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by fiber photometry data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The average maximum amplitude at Shaping (0.27±0.04) was significantly smaller compared to Early Learning (1.04±0.12), Late Learning (1.58±0.18), and Expert (1.59±0.17).
source: Further, the average maximum amplitude at Shaping (0.27±0.04) was significantly smaller compared to Early Learning (1.04±0.12, p=0.0190), Late Learning (1.58±0.18, p=0.0061), and Expert (1.59±0.17, p=0.0052).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of fiber photometry data.

claim: Calcium activity regressed to Shaping levels during the Reward session.
source: We observed that calcium activity regressed to Shaping levels and was significantly smaller than Early (p=0.0306), Late (p=0.0126), and Expert (p=0.0098).
evidence: This claim is supported by fiber photometry data during the Reward session.

claim: auROC values significantly increased across learning.
source: As with the maximum calcium amplitude, auROC values significantly increased across learning (F(2.162,8.650)=51.17, p<0.0001, n=5; Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by fiber photometry data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: auROC values at Shaping (0.54±0.01) were significantly lower than Early Learning (0.70±0.03), Late Learning (0.83±0.03), and Expert (0.85±0.02), but not Reward (0.57±0.01).
source: Notably, auROC values at Shaping (0.54±0.01) were significantly lower than Early Learning (0.70±0.03, p=0.0116), Late Learning (0.83±0.03, p=0.0017), and Expert (0.85±0.02, p=0.0007), but not Reward (0.57±0.01, p=0.4111).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of fiber photometry data.

claim: Pupil and POm activity were tightly correlated but decoupled during the PT window.
source: Similar to previous studies (Petty et al., 2021; La Terra et al., 2022), we found that pupil and POm activity were tightly correlated but decoupled during the PT window with POm activity immediately regressing to baseline, while pupil activity remained elevated (Figure 3A and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by simultaneous recording of POm calcium signals and pupil dynamics shown in Figure 3A and G.

claim: Pupil dilation lagged POm activity by ~250ms on average.
source: Pupil dilation lagged by ~250ms on average (Figure 3H)
evidence: This claim is supported by cross-correlation analysis shown in Figure 3H.

claim: POm axonal activity remained strikingly consistent between the Go and NoGo conditions.
source: Conversely, POm axonal activity remained strikingly consistent between the Go and NoGo conditions (Figure 3J).
evidence: This claim is supported by fiber photometry data shown in Figure 3J.

claim: The main effect of behavioral time points was significant for maximum calcium amplitude, but the main effect of presented texture was not.
source: The main effect of behavioral time points was significant (F (4,32)=57.16, p<0.0001), but the main effect of presented texture was not (F (1,8)=0.3797, p=0.5549; Figure 3K).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of fiber photometry data shown in Figure 3K.

claim: Despite divergent licking and pupil activity as a function of the presented texture, axonal calcium activity remained unchanged.
source: Thus, despite divergent licking and pupil activity as a function of the presented texture, axonal calcium activity remained unchanged, indicating POm-striatal projections do not encode vibrissae-specific sensory information.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the fiber photometry data comparing Go and NoGo trials.

claim: POm-striatal projections do not encode vibrissae-specific sensory information.
source: Thus, despite divergent licking and pupil activity as a function of the presented texture, axonal calcium activity remained unchanged, indicating POm-striatal projections do not encode vibrissae-specific sensory information.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the fiber photometry data comparing Go and NoGo trials.

claim: Calcium activity remained remarkably consistent across different trial outcomes.
source: Upon segmentation by trial outcome (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G–J), licking and pupil dynamics exhibited discrete outcome-dependent activity patterns (Lee and Margolis, 2016), but calcium activity again remained remarkably consistent (Figure 3M–P).
evidence: This claim is supported by fiber photometry data shown in Figure 3M–P.

claim: POm-striatal projections do not appear to encode texture- or outcome-specific information.
source: Overall, POm-striatal projections do not appear to encode texture- or outcome-specific information, suggesting that POm may represent a behaviorally relevant arousal-related role.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the fiber photometry data across different trial types and outcomes.

claim: Photoinactivation of POm-striatal axons during the Learning phase resulted in the JAWS cohort requiring significantly more sessions (12.50±0.50 sessions) to attain Expert status compared to the FP cohort (7.60±0.51 sessions) and No Stim cohort (7.40±0.24 sessions).
source: However, photoinactivation of POm-striatal axons during the Learning phase resulted in the JAWS cohort requiring significantly more sessions (12.50±0.50 sessions, n=4 mice) to attain Expert status compared to the other two cohorts with different experimental conditions (FP with constant illumination across the entire session: 7.60±0.51 sessions, n=5 mice; No Stim with no illumination: 7.40±0.24 sessions, n=5 mice) (F(3,11) = 8.542, p=0.0041, JAWS vs. FP p=0.0470; JAWS vs. No Stim p=0.0202; FP vs. No Stim p>0.9999; Figure 4I–J).
evidence: This claim is supported by optogenetic inhibition experiments shown in Figure 4I–J.

claim: Photoinactivation resulted in a decrease in overall responding (Bias) during the Learning phase.
source: The only significant effect was a decrease in overall responding (Bias) during the Learning phase (Off: 0.56±0.32, On: 0.48±0.32, p=0.0351).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral analysis during optogenetic inhibition.

claim: The average RT was significantly slower in the On condition (Off: 0.87±0.07, On: 0.93±0.07, p=0.0124).
source: Due to this, we assessed if inhibition resulted in slower RTs and found that the average RT was significantly slower in the On condition (Off: 0.87±0.07, On: 0.93±0.07, p=0.0124).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral analysis during optogenetic inhibition.

claim: The suppression of this behaviorally relevant arousal signal resulted in more learning sessions due to delayed RTs.
source: Thus, the suppression of this behaviorally relevant arousal signal resulted in more learning sessions due to delayed RTs.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the optogenetic inhibition results.

claim: POm could provide an early salience- or arousal-related 'priming' signal to the pDLS that interacts with subsequent corticostriatal signals, leading up to behavioral action selection.
source: We propose that POm could provide an early salience- or arousal-related 'priming' signal to the pDLS that interacts with subsequent corticostriatal signals, leading up to behavioral action selection.
evidence: This is a proposed interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: POm inputs likely arrive in striatum with shorter latency than cortical inputs following whisker stimulation.
source: POm inputs likely arrive in striatum with shorter latency than cortical inputs following whisker stimulation (Smith et al., 2012; Alloway et al., 2017; Alloway et al., 2014; Mowery et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: POm provides large amplitude PSPs to D1- and D2-SPNs, of similar amplitude to previously measured M1 inputs and larger amplitude than S1 inputs.
source: We found that POm provides large amplitude PSPs to D1- and D2-SPNs, of similar amplitude to previously measured M1 inputs and larger amplitude than S1 inputs (Lee et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from this study and comparison to prior literature.

claim: The equally strong innervation of D1- and D2-SPN is consistent with previous work on the co-activation of SPN populations during natural movements.
source: This equally strong innervation of D1- and D2-SPN is consistent with previous work on the co-activation of SPN populations during natural movements (Cui et al., 2013; Tecuapetla et al., 2014; Klaus et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison to prior literature.

claim: Striatal PV cells are thought to provide feedforward inhibition to surrounding neurons via short-latency GABAergic synaptic signals.
source: Striatal PV cells are thought to provide feedforward inhibition to surrounding neurons via short-latency GABAergic synaptic signals (Tepper et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Stimulation of a presynaptic PV cell in synaptically coupled PV-SPN paired recordings causes GABA-mediated depolarization in the postsynaptic SPN when the SPN's resting potentials was negative.
source: Stimulation of a presynaptic PV cell in synaptically coupled PV-SPN paired recordings causes GABA-mediated depolarization in the postsynaptic SPN when the SPN's resting potentials was negative (Koós and Tepper, 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The chloride equilibrium potential is surprisingly positive in adult striatal SPNs, closer to –60 mV compared to the more typical –80 mV.
source: Indeed, recent work found that the chloride equilibrium potential is surprisingly positive in adult striatal SPNs, closer to –60 mV compared to the more typical –80 mV (Day et al., 2024)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: When GABA-mediated depolarization was paired with further glutamate-evoked depolarization, the probability of action potential firing was increased.
source: In Day et al., 2024, when GABA-mediated depolarization was paired with further glutamate-evoked depolarization, the probability of action potential firing was increased, suggesting that GABA-mediated depolarization was excitatory rather than shunting (Day et al., 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The striatum receives inputs from myriad subcortical regions including other thalamic nuclei and external globus pallidus.
source: For example, the striatum receives inputs from myriad subcortical regions including other thalamic nuclei (Hunnicutt et al., 2016; Mandelbaum et al., 2019) and external globus pallidus (Mastro et al., 2014; Baker et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: vZI and APT efficiently shunt incoming sensory information via feedforward inhibition onto POm neurons.
source: All three nuclei receive ascending spinal trigeminal (whisker-related sensory) inputs, but vZI and APT efficiently shunt incoming sensory information via feedforward inhibition onto POm neurons (Lavallée et al., 2005; Trageser and Keller, 2004; Trageser et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: This inhibitory gating is overcome by arousal-related cholinergic suppression of presynaptic GABA release within POm.
source: This inhibitory gating is overcome by (1) arousal-related cholinergic suppression of presynaptic GABA release within POm (Masri et al., 2006)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: This inhibitory gating is overcome by convergence of bottom-up and top-down signals within a specified temporal window.
source: or (2) convergence of bottom-up and top-down signals within a specified temporal window (Groh et al., 2014; Miller-Hansen and Sherman, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: POm receives direct glutamatergic input from superior colliculus that enhances sensory responses.
source: In addition to cholinergic, cortical, and subcortical GABAergic afferents, POm also receives direct glutamatergic input from superior colliculus (SC) that enhances sensory responses (Roger and Cadusseau, 1984; Gharaei et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: SC is a region implicated in attentional orienting of either somatosensory or visually relevant stimuli.
